info.text: How a three-year campaign to clear the Drina valley produced the refugee crowd inside Srebrenica's 'safe area,' and how the mandate, chain of command, and dual-key air-support system meant to protect that area gave way in July 1995 to finish what the campaign had already set out to do.

clusters.name: Inside the Enclave
clusters.fact: The town's population swelled from roughly 9,000 to more than 40,000 as refugees fled a three-year campaign of ethnic cleansing across the surrounding valley, living on dwindling food under near-daily shelling -- and when the enclave finally fell in July 1995, the promised safety ended not in rescue but in women and children bused away while men and boys were pulled aside to be killed.

constant shelling.text: Srebrenica and the Potočari compound were subjected to near-daily artillery and sniper fire for three years, intensifying sharply during the final 1995 offensive.

food scarcity.text: The besieged enclave depended on infrequent, often-blocked UN aid convoys; by 1995 hunger and malnutrition were routine for the population sheltering there.

refugee overcrowding.text: Srebrenica's population swelled from roughly 9,000 before the war to more than 40,000 by 1993 as Bosniaks fled ethnic cleansing throughout the Drina valley; by the evening of July 11, 1995, some 20,000-25,000 had converged on the Dutch compound at Potočari alone.

separation of men and boys.text: As refugees were evacuated from Potočari, Bosnian Serb forces pulled men and teenage boys from the crowd for what became the mass killings later ruled genocide.

info.text: Refugees converged on the Dutch compound at Potočari as the town fell -- the last stop before the crowd was forcibly divided by sex and age.

clusters.name: A Mandate With No Teeth
clusters.fact: Dutchbat's own mandate had disarmed the population it was sent to protect in exchange for a promise of UN protection, while its rules of engagement left roughly 400 lightly armed soldiers too narrowly authorized, and eventually too exposed as hostages, to resist an army willing to overrun their positions one by one.

demilitarization agreement.text: A 1993 arrangement under which Bosniak defenders in Srebrenica surrendered heavy weapons to the UN in exchange for protection as a demilitarized safe area -- protection the enclave's own defenders no longer had the means to provide themselves.

hostage-taking of peacekeepers.text: On July 9-11, 1995, Bosnian Serb forces took roughly 30 Dutch soldiers hostage and threatened to kill them in direct response to the one NATO airstrike that did occur, forcing its suspension.

overrun observation posts.text: Dutchbat's forward observation posts, including Foxtrot, were overrun one by one during the July 1995 offensive, with soldiers withdrawing, surrendering, or being taken hostage.

rules of engagement.text: The mission's authorization to use force, calibrated for a consent-based peacekeeping presence rather than combat -- it permitted little beyond self-defense even as an organized offensive advanced.

info.text: The lightly armed Dutch UN battalion stationed at Srebrenica from 1994, tasked with protecting the enclave under a peacekeeping mandate that gave it almost no capacity to fight.

clusters.name: Permission Withheld
clusters.fact: Behind the 'safe area' sat a Security Council resolution with no enforcement plan of its own, a secret pact among Western capitals to stop bombing Bosnian Serb positions, a general who twice hesitated over the one strike that might have mattered, and, when permission finally came, a request that arrived too late because it had been filed on the wrong form.

Bernard Janvier's hesitation.text: The French general commanding UN forces in the former Yugoslavia initially declined, then only reluctantly approved, Dutchbat's July 1995 requests for close air support.

NATO airstrikes suspended.text: In late May 1995, US, French, and British leaders privately agreed to suspend NATO airstrikes against Bosnian Serb forces without informing Dutch officials, despite earlier commitments to provide air support within two hours if an enclave was attacked.

Security Council Resolution 819.text: Adopted April 16, 1993, this resolution demanded Srebrenica be treated as a 'safe area' free from armed attack -- the world's first civilian safe area declaration, with no accompanying enforcement mechanism.

misrouted request form.text: On the morning of July 11, 1995, Dutchbat's renewed request for close air support was rejected on procedural grounds -- submitted on the wrong form -- delaying approval by hours as the town fell.

info.text: The chain of UN and NATO commanders and diplomats whose approval was required before Dutchbat's request for air support could become an actual airstrike.

clusters.name: The Corridor
clusters.fact: Three years before the enclave fell, the Bosnian Serb assembly had already declared eliminating the Drina as a border between Serb states a strategic goal, and raids launched from inside the enclave by its own defenders gave Mladić's forces a pretext for finishing it -- a goal a March 1995 directive would order completed by making daily life for Srebrenica's people 'unbearable.'

Directive 7.text: Signed by Republika Srpska president Radovan Karadžić on March 8, 1995, this directive ordered VRS troops to create 'an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival' for Srebrenica's and Žepa's inhabitants -- the planning document behind the July offensive.

Drina Corps.text: The VRS army corps responsible for the eastern Bosnia front, tasked with executing the strategic goal against Srebrenica and, that July, Operation Krivaja 95; its deputy commander during the assault, Radislav Krstić, later became the first person the ICTY convicted of genocide.

Naser Orić's raids.text: Bosniak forces commanded by Naser Orić, based in the Srebrenica enclave, raided and destroyed dozens of surrounding Serb villages between 1992 and early 1993, killing Serb civilians and giving Bosnian Serb commanders a grievance they cited for years afterward.

Strategic Objective No. 3.text: One of six strategic objectives the Bosnian Serb assembly declared in May 1992: establishing a corridor along the Drina River valley by eliminating it as a border between Republika Srpska and Serbia -- a goal that required removing the Bosniak communities living in that valley.

info.text: The three-year siege and ethnic-cleansing campaign in the Drina river valley that preceded, and set the strategic terms for, Srebrenica's fall in July 1995.

bridges.fact: In April 1993 the Security Council declared Srebrenica the world's first civilian 'safe area,' demanding it be free from any hostile act -- a designation that promised protection without ever resourcing an actual defense, so refugees kept arriving on the strength of a word the Council itself had never made good.

info.text: The UN's formal designation for Srebrenica and several other besieged towns, created by Resolution 819 and never matched with the military means to enforce it.

bridges.fact: Dutchbat's commander requested close air support nine times as the Bosnian Serb offensive advanced -- a plea that had to climb through Dutchbat's own chain of command and then through NATO and the UN's joint 'dual key' authorization before a single strike could be approved, arriving, when it arrived at all, too late to matter.

info.text: The specific military request Dutchbat kept filing and resubmitting -- a mechanism this puzzle traces through its approval chain rather than a topic worth studying on its own.

bridges.fact: Nearly a decade after the killing, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia ruled that the murder of thousands of Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica met the legal definition of genocide -- still the only genocide conviction the tribunal ever returned, delivered long after the word could have changed anything happening on the ground.

info.text: The intentional destruction of a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group, in whole or in part -- the crime the ICTY found had been committed at Srebrenica.

bridges.fact: Between April 1992 and early 1993, a VRS directive ordered forces to inflict enough losses on Bosniak communities across the Drina valley to drive them out entirely -- the refugees who fled toward Srebrenica rather than be killed or expelled elsewhere were the overcrowding the town could never absorb.

info.text: The systematic effort to forcibly remove a population from a territory until it is ethnically homogeneous -- the campaign that produced Srebrenica's refugee crisis years before the 'safe area' was ever declared.

bridges.fact: On July 6, 1995, the VRS Drina Corps launched Operation Krivaja 95 -- the codename for the assault that began overrunning Dutchbat's observation posts one by one, the operational execution, at last, of a strategic goal the Bosnian Serb assembly had set three years earlier.

info.text: The Bosnian Serb Army's codename for its July 1995 offensive against the Srebrenica enclave.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts are decisions, campaigns, or agreements from 1992 or 1993 -- one to three years before Dutchbat's final week -- rather than something that happened during the five days of the assault itself?
lenses.explanation: Republika Srpska's assembly set its strategic goal, and Bosniak raids gave Mladić's command its pretext, three years before the offensive; the Security Council's resolution and Dutchbat's disarmament deal were both concluded within the same 1992-93 window, before any of the July 1995 crisis had begun.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts are a specific, dated political or diplomatic resolution, pact, or arrangement -- negotiated or declared by an authority before or during the crisis -- rather than a legal ruling handed down afterward or a description of a condition on the ground?
lenses.explanation: Each of these is a specific political instrument, not a retrospective judgment or a bare condition: a Security Council resolution, the 'safe area' status it created, a 1993 disarmament deal, and a secret 1995 pact among Western capitals to stop bombing -- four separate decisions layered on top of each other before the enclave ever fell. The genocide ruling belongs to a different category: it was adjudicated years later, not negotiated or declared in the moment.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts are directly about a request for help moving through someone else's chain of approval, and the specific points where that chain gave way?
lenses.explanation: Close air support had to be requested, escalated, and approved through a multi-party chain; the mission's own rules of engagement limited what could even be requested, the threat to Dutch hostages forced one approved strike to be called off, a commander's own hesitation slowed approval at the top, and a request literally filed on the wrong form cost the hours that mattered most.

reasons.Bernard Janvier's hesitation: The officer whose approval the request needed most was himself one of the chain's points of delay.

lenses.prompt: Which concepts, however real or eventually honored, only functioned as protection or accountability in hindsight -- arriving, being declared, or being ruled on well after the outcome they addressed was already decided?
lenses.explanation: A strategic goal declared in 1992, a 'safe area' declared with no enforcement plan in 1993, a general's hesitation on the days that decided the enclave's fate, and a genocide ruling delivered nearly a decade after the killing: each was real, and each mattered only in hindsight, once the outcome it addressed was already decided.

learningIntroduction.title: Before You Begin: Three Years, Not Five Days
learningIntroduction.summary: Context on the 1992 strategic goal and ethnic-cleansing campaign, the 1993 'safe area' designation, and the chain of command that failed Srebrenica in July 1995.

content.text:
## Three years, not five days

The five days in July 1995 usually get the story: nine requests for air support, a misfiled form, a general's hesitation. But the machinery that made those five days catastrophic had been assembling since 1992.

In May of that year, the Bosnian Serb assembly declared eliminating the Drina River as a border between "Serb states" a strategic goal -- language that required removing the Bosniak population from the valley it ran through. A VRS directive that November ordered forces to inflict enough losses on Drina valley communities to drive them out entirely. Tens of thousands who survived fled toward Srebrenica rather than the surrounding villages being burned around them; the town's population swelled from about 9,000 to more than 40,000. Bosniak forces based in the enclave, in turn, staged their own raids on nearby Serb villages -- killing hundreds and giving Bosnian Serb commanders a grievance they would cite for years.

By April 1993, with the enclave in crisis, the UN declared it the world's first civilian "safe area." The designation didn't end the siege; it just meant the siege continued under a UN flag, for two more years, until a March 1995 directive ordered troops to make life in Srebrenica "unbearable" and a July offensive finished what 1992's strategic goal had set out to do.

**Before you start:** how much of what follows in this puzzle was a five-day failure, and how much was a three-year plan working as intended?
